cards.rueckseite:
For alert (GCS 15), stable trauma patients:
1. **High-risk factor → imaging:** age **≥ 65**, **dangerous mechanism** (fall ≥ 3 ft/5 stairs, axial load, high-speed or rollover MVC, ejection, bicycle collision), **paresthesias** in the extremities
2. **Low-risk factor allowing range-of-motion test:** simple rear-end MVC, sitting in the ED, ambulatory at any time, delayed onset of neck pain, no midline tenderness
3. **Able to actively rotate the neck 45° left and right** → no imaging

More sensitive and specific than NEXUS (NEXUS is in the Board Review deck).

cards.vorderseite: Clearing the cervical spine in the obtunded patient
cards.rueckseite:
- **High-quality thin-cut CT** (with sagittal/coronal reconstructions) is the recommended study; a **normal CT** is generally sufficient to remove the collar (guideline level II/III)
- MRI within 48–72 h is an option if doubt persists or neurologic deficit is unexplained (finds ligamentous injury of uncertain significance)
- **Dynamic flexion–extension** X-rays/fluoroscopy are **not recommended** in obtunded patients
- Prolonged collars cause pressure ulcers, raised ICP, aspiration, difficult airway care

zeilen: Neck pain, stiffness or tenderness only; no physical signs
Neck complaints + **musculoskeletal signs** (reduced ROM, point tenderness)
Neck complaints + **neurologic signs** (reduced reflexes, weakness, sensory deficit)
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 1119–1120. Grades I–II: early mobilization, analgesia, avoid prolonged soft collar.

cards.vorderseite: Pediatric cervical spine: normal variants vs. injury
cards.rueckseite:
- **Pseudosubluxation:** physiologic anterior displacement of **C2 on C3** (≤ 3–4 mm, also C3 on C4) up to ≈ 8–10 yrs; check **Swischuk line** (posterior cervical line C1–C3: spinolaminar line of C2 should be within 1–2 mm)
- **ADI** normal up to **5 mm** in children (adults 3 mm)
- Unfused synchondroses (dens base until ≈ 7 yrs) mimic fractures
- Prevertebral soft tissue varies with crying/expiration
- Children < 8–9 yrs: fulcrum at **C2–C3**, more upper cervical and ligamentous injuries, AOD, **SCIWORA**
- Large occiput: use a board with occipital recess or shoulder roll

cards.vorderseite: SCIWORA (spinal cord injury without radiographic abnormality)
cards.rueckseite:
Objective SCI with normal X-rays/CT; mainly **children < 8 years** (elastic ligaments allow transient displacement); in adults usually central cord syndrome with spondylosis.
**MRI** often shows cord edema/hemorrhage or ligamentous injury (no MRI abnormality = better prognosis).
Up to 50% have **delayed onset** of deficits (hours to days).
**Management:** external immobilization (collar) for **12 weeks**, avoid high-risk activities for 6 months; flexion–extension films to exclude instability.

cards.text: **Atlanto-occipital dislocation** on CT/X-ray: basion–dens interval (BDI) and basion–axial interval (BAI) should each be ≤ {{c1::12 mm}} (Harris "rule of 12"); the {{c2::Powers ratio}} (basion–posterior C1 arch ÷ opisthion–anterior C1 arch) > 1 indicates anterior dislocation; in children the {{c3::occipital condyle–C1 interval}} is the preferred measure. Treatment: {{c4::occipitocervical fusion}}; **traction is contraindicated**.

cards.vorderseite: Transverse atlantal ligament injury: Dickman classification
cards.rueckseite:
- **Type I (anatomic):** tear within the ligament substance (Ia midportion, Ib periosteal insertion) → **will not heal** → **early C1–C2 fusion**
- **Type II (physiologic):** **avulsion of the C1 tubercle** (bony) → can heal with **rigid immobilization (halo/collar)** in ≈ 74%; fuse if still unstable after 3–4 months

Diagnosis: MRI (ligament), CT (tubercle avulsion). Indirect sign: lateral mass overhang > 6.9 mm (rule of Spence) or ADI > 3 mm in adults.

cards.text: Anterior atlantoaxial subluxation: normal **atlantodental interval (ADI)** is ≤ {{c1::3 mm}} in adults and ≤ {{c2::5 mm}} in children. ADI 3–5 mm in adults suggests {{c3::TAL disruption}}; > 5 mm suggests additional {{c4::alar ligament}} injury. In rheumatoid arthritis, the {{c5::posterior atlantodental interval}} better predicts myelopathy (PADI < 14 mm = risk).

cards.vorderseite: Combined C1 and C2 fractures: treatment
cards.rueckseite:
Treatment is usually dictated by the **C2 fracture**:
- C1 + type II odontoid fracture with **dens displacement ≥ 6 mm** (or age > 50) → surgical stabilization (C1–C2 fusion; odontoid screw not possible if C1 ring broken)
- C1 + type III odontoid or hangman fracture → mostly external immobilization (halo/collar)
- Intact TAL is key for C1 ring injuries
Combined injuries are more often unstable than either alone.

- Gardner–Wells tongs: pins **above the pinna, in line with the external auditory meatus** (slightly posterior for flexion)
- **Starting weight ≈ 10 lb (head) + 5 lb per level** below; increase by 5–10 lb with lateral X-ray and neuro exam after each increase
- **Contraindications:** **atlanto-occipital dislocation**, distraction injuries (type IIa hangman), skull fractures at the pin sites
- Awake, examinable patient: reduction without prior MRI acceptable (MRI before reduction in obtunded patients or before open reduction because of possible disc herniation)
- BDI should remain ≤ 12 mm (overdistraction)

cards.text: Timing of decompression after acute SCI: surgery within {{c1::24 h}} is associated with better motor/sensory scores and a higher chance of {{c2::≥ 2-grade AIS improvement}} (STASCIS: 19.8% vs. 8.8%); the benefit is largest in the {{c3::upper extremities}} in cervical SCI. **Hypothermia** for SCI is {{c4::not recommended}} outside trials.

cards.vorderseite: VTE prophylaxis in spinal cord injury
cards.rueckseite:
DVT risk very high (up to 50–100% subclinical, highest in the first 2 weeks).
- **LMWH** (or adjusted-dose heparin) **within 72 h** once bleeding risk allows, plus SCDs/stockings
- Duration ≈ **3 months**
- Low-dose heparin alone is insufficient
- **IVC filter not routine**; only if anticoagulation fails or is contraindicated

cards.titel: White and Panjabi checklist for clinical instability (lower cervical spine)
zeilen: Anterior elements destroyed or unable to function
Posterior elements destroyed or unable to function
Sagittal plane rotation > 11° (relative to adjacent level)

cards.vorderseite: Hyperflexion sprain and delayed cervical instability
cards.rueckseite:
**Hyperflexion sprain:** disruption of the posterior ligamentous complex (± capsules, PLL) without fracture; initial films may be normal or show only **mild kyphosis, fanning of spinous processes**, widened facets.
**Delayed instability** in up to 20–50% of missed injuries (neck pain, progressive kyphosis).
**Action:** MRI (STIR) or delayed flexion–extension films (after muscle spasm subsides, ≈ 2 weeks) in patients with persistent pain; collar meanwhile; posterior fusion if unstable.

Severe **flexion–compression** injury (C4–C7): oblique vertebral body fracture from the anterosuperior to the inferior endplate, **retrolisthesis** of the posterior body into the canal, disruption of disc, PLL and posterior ligaments → **three-column injury**, often with anterior cord syndrome.
Differs from a teardrop fracture by the larger anterior fragment involving the whole body height.
**Treatment:** unstable → **corpectomy with anterior plating, usually plus posterior fixation**.

- **Cervical cord neurapraxia** (transient quadriparesis/paresthesias < 15 min to 48 h): canal stenosis contributes; recurrence ≈ 56% on return; MRI required
- **Stinger/burner:** unilateral burning arm pain C5–C6 (brachial plexus traction or foraminal root compression); not a cord injury
- **Burning hands syndrome:** bilateral → mild central cord injury
- **Spear tackler's spine:** stenosis + loss of lordosis + prior traumatic changes + spearing technique → contraindication to collision sports
- Do **not remove the football helmet** in the field (remove face mask)

zeilen: Wedge compression of one endplate / split (pincer) fracture
Posterior tension band failure through bone (Chance) or ligaments
Anterior tension band failure (hyperextension), e.g., ankylosed spine
cards.notiz: Greenberg ch. 72 (thoracolumbar fractures), p. 1200–1206. Modifiers: neurologic status (N0–N4, NX) and M1 (indeterminate PLC injury), M2 (comorbidity such as AS).

cards.rueckseite:
**Osteoporosis:** DEXA **T-score ≤ −2.5** (osteopenia −1 to −2.5); a fragility fracture defines it clinically.
**Work-up:** exclude malignancy (MRI: convex posterior wall, pedicle involvement, epidural mass, diffuse T1 low signal suggest tumor; myeloma screen).
**Treatment:** analgesia, brief bracing, mobilization; **vertebroplasty/kyphoplasty** for persistent pain from an unhealed fracture (bone marrow edema on STIR); surgery for instability, neurologic deficit or progressive kyphosis.
Treat the osteoporosis (vitamin D, calcium, bisphosphonate, denosumab, teriparatide). **Kümmell disease:** delayed collapse with an intravertebral vacuum cleft.

zeilen: ≈ 6%; occasionally L5 root (caught between fragment and L5 transverse process)
≈ 28%; unilateral L5/S1/S2 radiculopathy (sciatica), bladder rarely affected
Through the central sacral canal (incl. transverse and U/H-shaped fractures)
cards.notiz: Greenberg Table 72.7, p. 1216. U-shaped fracture = **spinopelvic dissociation** (jumper's fracture) → lumbopelvic fixation.

cards.rueckseite:
Usually **mechanically stable** (no ligamentous disruption); steroids not indicated.
**Surgery indicated for:** progressive neurologic deficit with canal compromise, **CSF fistula**, retained bullet causing compression (especially **cauda equina T12–L5**: removal improves motor recovery), copper jacket (toxic), infection, rare instability.
Complete cord injury: decompression does not help.
**Antibiotics** (broad-spectrum, 7–14 days) when the bullet passed through **bowel/colon** before the spine. Lead toxicity if the bullet lies in a joint/disc space (synovial fluid).

zeilen: Angle of mandible to skull base
Distal ICA, vertebral artery; difficult access → endovascular
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 1219–1220. Hard signs (expanding hematoma, active bleeding, bruit/thrill, deficit) → OR; stable patients → CTA.

cards.vorderseite: Delayed neurologic deterioration after spinal cord injury
cards.rueckseite:
- **Posttraumatic syringomyelia** (≈ 3–4% clinically, more on MRI; months to years later): ascending sensory level, pain, new weakness, loss of reflexes above the injury → arachnolysis/expansile duraplasty or syrinx shunt
- **Tethering/arachnoiditis**, myelomalacia
- Progressive kyphosis/instability, adjacent stenosis
- Early (days): cord edema ascending ("ascending deterioration"), hypotension, hypoxia, vertebral artery thrombosis, over-distraction

- Diaphragm = **C3–C5** (phrenic): injuries at or above C3 need ventilation; C4–C5 often need temporary support
- Loss of intercostal and abdominal muscles → weak cough, atelectasis, pneumonia (leading cause of death)
- Monitor **vital capacity**: < 15 mL/kg (or < 1 L) or falling → intubation; deterioration often in the first 3–5 days as cord edema ascends
- Vagal stimulation during suctioning → bradycardia/asystole (atropine)
- Supine VC is better than upright in tetraplegia (abdominal binder helps)
- Diaphragmatic pacing for high lesions with intact phrenic nerves

cards.vorderseite: Spinal shock, neurogenic shock and the bulbocavernosus reflex
cards.rueckseite:
- **Spinal shock:** transient loss of all reflexes and tone below the injury (hours to days); completeness of SCI cannot be judged until it resolves
- **Bulbocavernosus reflex** (squeeze glans/clitoris or tug the catheter → anal sphincter contraction, S3–S4): return marks the end of spinal shock (usually within 24–48 h); absent BC reflex with conus/cauda lesions
- **Neurogenic shock:** loss of sympathetic tone with lesions above **T6** → **hypotension with bradycardia**, warm skin; treat with fluids, **pressors with α + β activity** (norepinephrine), atropine for bradycardia; exclude hemorrhagic shock first
